title: Music Genres Around the World
subtitle: Every genre is a place, a history and a rhythm you can name.
objectives: Define what a music genre is
Match six major genres to the countries they came from
Describe the characteristic rhythm or instruments of each
Explain how migration and trade spread musical styles
Use the elements of music to describe a genre

cards.title: A genre is a place with a beat attached
cards.text: Nobody sat down and invented reggae. It grew in one place, out of what was already there, and then it travelled.

cards.title: What makes a genre a genre
cards.text: A genre is a family of music that shares habits. Recognising one is the same skill as recognising a car by its shape.
points: **A typical rhythm** you could clap without the record.
**A typical set of instruments.**
**A place and a time** it came from.
**Rules you can break** once everyone knows them.

cards.title: Where each one is from
cards.text: Tap through. Several quiz questions come from this.

question.text: Which country did reggae come from?
question.explain: Jamaica, from the 1960s. The giveaway is the guitar chopping on the offbeat.

cards.title: Rhythm gives it away before anything else
cards.text: You usually know the genre within two bars, and it is almost never the melody that told you.
points: **Reggae** puts the guitar on the *offbeat*.
**Samba** stacks percussion over a fast two-beat pulse.
**Flamenco** counts in cycles, with handclaps holding it.
**Hip hop** is built on a looped drum break.

cards.title: Racing games sort their radio by genre
cards.text: Different stations, different feel, same road. That is a genre doing its job: setting an expectation in seconds.
points: **You pick a station** for the drive you want.
**Two bars in**, you know if it fits.
**Tempo and texture** are doing that, not the words.
**Genre is a shortcut** to a mood.

question.text: Hip hop grew out of DJs doing what?
options: Looping the drum break in a record
question.explain: The break is the part where the drums play alone. Looping it made a new music out of old records.

cards.title: Good spot to pause
cards.text: Six genres named. Part 2 is how they moved, and how to describe one properly. Your place is saved.

cards.title: Genres move the way people move
cards.text: Almost every genre on that list is a record of somebody's journey, forced or chosen.

cards.title: Trade, migration and empire
cards.text: Three forces spread music around the world, and none of them were about music.
points: **Samba** carries West African rhythm into Brazil.
**Reggae** grew where Caribbean and American radio met.
**Flamenco** blends Roma, Andalusian and North African roots.
**Music remembers the route** long after the map changes.

cards.title: A genre is evidence
cards.text: If you can hear West African drumming in Brazilian music, you have found a fact about history in a sound.
points: **Nobody wrote it down.** It survived by being played.
**Instruments travel** even when people cannot.
**A rhythm outlasts an empire.**
**That is worth knowing** before you dismiss any of it.

question.text: Which genre uses a full orchestra of tuned bronze gongs?
question.explain: Gamelan, from Indonesia. Whole ensembles of gongs and metal keys, tuned to each other.

cards.title: How to describe a genre properly
cards.text: Use the elements from Week 1. Four sentences will do it, and they beat saying it slaps.
points: **Tempo** — roughly how fast?
**Rhythm** — where do the strong beats land?
**Timbre** — which instruments carry it?
**Form** — does it repeat, build, or wander?

cards.title: Game soundtracks borrow genres on purpose
cards.text: A game set in a city sounds nothing like one set in a wasteland. That difference is a genre choice, made by a person.
points: **Genre tells you where you are** before the art does.
**Change the score, change the place.**
**Same map can feel like two games.**
**Somebody chose that.** It is a job.

question.text: Which of these is NOT part of describing a genre?
options: How much you personally like it
question.explain: Liking it is a review, not a description. The other three are what actually define a genre.

cards.title: A walkout song is a genre decision
cards.text: Fighters pick the music the whole arena hears them arrive to. Nobody picks it by accident.
points: **It says where you are from**, often literally.
**Tempo sets the room's pulse.**
**A whole country's music** can walk out with one person.
**That is genre used as a flag.**

terms.def: A family of music sharing a typical rhythm, instruments, place and time.
The weak beat between the strong ones. Reggae puts the guitar there.
The part of a record where the drums play alone. Hip hop was built on looping it.
The repeating rhythmic cycle that flamenco is counted in.
An Indonesian ensemble of tuned bronze gongs and metal keys.
Instruments played by striking or shaking. Samba is carried by them.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **A genre = rhythm, instruments, place and time.**
**Reggae Jamaica · samba Brazil · flamenco Spain.**
**Hip hop the Bronx · K-pop Korea · gamelan Indonesia.**
**Genres travel** because people do.

quiz.text: What makes a group of songs a genre?
options: A shared rhythm, set of instruments, place and time
Being released in the same year
quiz.explain: Shared habits. That is why you can recognise one within a couple of bars.
quiz.objective: Define what a music genre is

quiz.explain: Brazil, carrying West African rhythm with it. Layers of percussion over a fast two-beat pulse.
quiz.objective: Match six major genres to the countries they came from

quiz.text: Flamenco comes from which part of which country?
quiz.explain: Andalusia. Guitar, handclaps and a singer, counted in repeating cycles called compás.
quiz.objective: Match six major genres to the countries they came from

quiz.text: Where and when did hip hop begin?
options: The Bronx, New York, in the 1970s
quiz.explain: The Bronx in the 1970s, out of DJs looping the drum break in existing records.
quiz.objective: Match six major genres to the countries they came from

quiz.text: What is the giveaway sound of reggae?
quiz.explain: The offbeat chop, with the bass leading the song. The other three belong to gamelan, flamenco and hip hop.
quiz.objective: Describe the characteristic rhythm or instruments of each

quiz.text: Which country is gamelan music from?
quiz.explain: Indonesia. A gamelan is a whole ensemble of tuned bronze gongs and metal keys.
quiz.objective: Match six major genres to the countries they came from

quiz.text: What is a break, in the hip hop sense?
options: The part of a record where the drums play alone
quiz.explain: The drum-only section. DJs looped it, and a whole genre grew out of that one idea.
quiz.objective: Describe the characteristic rhythm or instruments of each

quiz.text: How did West African rhythm end up in Brazilian music?
options: Through the movement of people across the Atlantic
It was invented separately in both places
It arrived with Portuguese classical music
quiz.explain: Music travels the way people do. The rhythm survived the crossing even where nothing was written down.
quiz.objective: Explain how migration and trade spread musical styles

quiz.text: Music can be evidence of historical movement between countries.
quiz.explain: True. Hearing West African drumming in Brazilian music is a fact about history preserved in sound.
quiz.objective: Explain how migration and trade spread musical styles

quiz.text: Which of these describes a genre rather than reviewing it?
quiz.explain: Tempo, instruments and origin are description. The rest is opinion, which is a different job.
quiz.objective: Use the elements of music to describe a genre

quiz.text: Which element of music tells you which instruments are carrying a genre?
quiz.explain: Timbre, the colour of the sound. It is how you tell a gamelan from a rondalla instantly.
quiz.objective: Use the elements of music to describe a genre

quiz.text: K-pop developed in which country, and from roughly when?
quiz.explain: South Korea, from the 1990s, built around groups, choreography and video from the start.
quiz.objective: Match six major genres to the countries they came from

teacher.summary: Week 2 MAPEH covers music genres around the world, matching the Term 1 weekly scope. It is built so that the genres are never just a list to memorise: each one is tied to a place, a rhythm and a route, and the second half makes the argument that a genre is historical evidence rather than a label. The worldGenres figure carries the six place-and-sound pairs so the cards can spend their space on why rather than what. The method card near the end is the transferable part — describing any genre with tempo, rhythm, timbre and form uses the Week 1 vocabulary and gives him something to say about music that is not an opinion.
discussion: Play thirty seconds of two of the six and ask him to name the difference using the elements. Tempo and timbre will get him most of the way.
Ask him what a genre tells you about a place. Samba and reggae both have honest answers.
Ask him to pick a walkout song and justify it with tempo and instruments rather than with liking it.
Ask why hip hop needed the turntable to exist. It is the clearest case of a technology creating a genre.
teacher.extension: Have him build a six-track playlist, one per genre, and write one sentence per track using only tempo, rhythm, timbre and form. Banning the word 'good' is the whole exercise.
misconceptions: 'A genre is decided by who sings it.' It is decided by shared rhythm, instruments, place and time.
'Genres were invented by record companies.' Most grew in a place first and were labelled afterwards.
'Describing music means saying whether it is good.' Description uses the elements. Liking it is a separate question.
'Reggae and samba are basically the same because both use drums.' The rhythms are completely different, and that is what a genre is.
